questions.q: Which signature has a type parameter that does not earn its place?
questions.explain: In logAll, T appears once and connects nothing; readonly unknown[] says the same thing more simply. In the others, the type parameter links an input to an output or to another argument.
options: function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined
function logAll<T>(items: readonly T[]): void
function indexBy<T, K>(items: readonly T[], keyOf: (item: T) => K): Map<K, T>
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][]

questions.q: Why is function parseJson<T>(text: string): T dangerous?
questions.explain: A return-only type parameter cannot be inferred from anything, so it just becomes whatever the caller writes. The honest signature returns unknown, followed by a guard or a validator.
options: Because generic functions are slow
Because T appears only in the return type, so the caller picks any type and nothing checks it: it is as T in disguise
Because JSON.parse cannot return objects
Because T must always have a default

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: The JSON holds the string "5000". The type parameter only told the compiler to call it a number, so + 100 joins text. Nothing checked the data.
options: string 5000100
number 5100
string 5100
A runtime error: kobo is not a number

questions.q: In function choose<C extends string>(allowed: readonly C[], fallback: NoInfer<C>): C, what does NoInfer do?
questions.explain: Without NoInfer, a fallback of "GBP" would widen C to include it. With it, "GBP" is rejected because it is not one of the allowed currencies.
options: It turns off type checking for fallback
It stops TypeScript from using fallback to infer C, so C comes from allowed alone and fallback is only checked against it
It makes fallback optional
It converts fallback to a string at runtime

questions.q: This compiles (no NoInfer). What does it print?
questions.explain: C was inferred from both arguments, so "GBP" is accepted as a fallback even though it is not allowed, and it is returned when nothing matches. NoInfer<C> on the fallback turns this into a compile error.
options: USD GBP
USD NGN
USD undefined
GBP GBP

questions.q: Why is groupBy(items, keyOf) a better parameter order than groupBy(keyOf, items)?
questions.explain: Inference works best when a value reveals the type parameter and callbacks are then contextually typed from it. With the callback first, its parameter may have to be annotated by hand.
options: Because TypeScript cannot infer anything from callbacks
Because T is inferred from items first, and the callback's parameter is then typed from T, which also gives it autocompletion
Because callbacks must always come first
Because arrays cannot be the second argument

questions.q: class Emitter<Events extends Record<string, unknown>> rejects interface BankEvents { "transfer.completed": { kobo: number } }. Why?
questions.explain: The constraint asked for more than the class needs. It only uses keyof Events and Events[K], so Events extends object is enough and accepts interfaces.
options: Interfaces cannot have quoted property names
Record<string, unknown> requires an index signature (any string key), and an interface only promises its listed keys
Event maps must be classes
The payload must be a primitive

questions.q: What is a good rule for choosing a constraint on a type parameter?
questions.explain: Too loose and the code cannot do its job (you cannot read item.id); too tight and good types are refused. T extends { id: Id } for a repository is the right size.
options: Always use extends any so every caller is accepted
Require exactly what the implementation uses, and nothing more
Always require Record<string, unknown>
Never use constraints; check the types at runtime

questions.q: Which declaration is invalid?
questions.explain: Type parameters with defaults must come after those without, just like optional function parameters. C = string before the required T is an error.
options: type Result<T, E = string> = …
interface Repository<T, Id = string> { … }
type Page<C = string, T> = …
class Cache<K = string, V = unknown> { … }

questions.q: With interface Repository<TEntity, TId = string, TCreateInput = Partial<TEntity>>, what is Repository<Account>?
questions.explain: Missing type arguments take their defaults, and a default may use earlier parameters: Partial<TEntity> becomes Partial<Account>. That is how @zudojs/database keeps its five-parameter contract short to use.
options: An error: all three type arguments are required
Repository<Account, string, Partial<Account>>
Repository<Account, unknown, unknown>
Repository<Account, Account, Account>

questions.q: What does findBy<K extends keyof T>(key: K, value: T[K]) guarantee?
questions.explain: K is inferred from the key, and T[K] is the type of that property. So findBy("frozen", "yes") is refused when frozen is a boolean.
options: That value is a string
That key is one of T's property names and value has that property's type
That the result is never empty
That key exists in the database at runtime

questions.explain: Two accounts are frozen, and one belongs to Ada. The generic keeps the full element type, so a.owner is known on the results.
options: Tunde,Eve 1
Ada 1
Tunde,Eve 3
Tunde 1

questions.q: Why does the repository's create take Omit<T, "id"> and update take Partial<Omit<T, "id">>?
questions.explain: Removing id from the input types makes "choose your own id" and "change an id" compile errors. Partial lets an update change only some fields.
options: To make the methods faster
So ids are always generated by the repository and can never be chosen or changed by a caller
Because id is not allowed in TypeScript objects
So the caller must pass every field when updating

questions.q: A patch arrived from JSON with an id the type did not allow. What does this print?
questions.explain: Later spreads win. Putting id last means a smuggled id in the patch is always overwritten, even when the types were bypassed at runtime.

questions.q: In the generic repository, create builds { ...input, id: this.nextId() } as T. Why is that assertion considered justified?
questions.explain: This is the "proof the compiler cannot follow" case. It sits in one place in shared code, where tests cover it, instead of being scattered across callers.
options: Because every assertion inside a class is safe
Because Omit<T, "id"> plus an id is a T for real entities, but TypeScript cannot prove it for an unknown generic T; the proof is local and tested
Because as T validates the object at runtime
Because T is always any inside a generic class

questions.q: Why should a generic findById return T | undefined rather than throw when nothing is found?
questions.explain: A lookup screen might show "no such account"; a transfer might treat it as a failure. Returning T | undefined, like Map.get, lets each caller decide, and the type forces them to.
options: Because throwing is not allowed in async functions
Because "not found" is a normal outcome, and only the caller knows whether it is an error in that situation
Because undefined is faster than an exception
Because TypeScript cannot type thrown errors

questions.q: What is the error type of andThen(r1, fn) when r1: Result<number, "invalid-amount"> and fn returns Result<Account, "account-not-found">?
questions.explain: andThen returns Result<U, E | F>: the chain can fail at either step, so the error type is the union of both. The types collect the possible failures for you.
options: "invalid-amount"
"account-not-found"
"invalid-amount" | "account-not-found"
string

questions.q: Why is err declared as function err<const E>(error: E): Result<never, E>?
questions.explain: A const type parameter infers the narrowest type, like an as const at the call site. Literal error codes are what make E a useful, closed union.
options: So errors cannot be changed after they are created
So err("insufficient-funds") keeps the literal type "insufficient-funds" instead of widening to string
Because const is required for every generic function
So err can only be called once

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map transforms the value of a success and passes a failure through untouched. The function never runs for the failed result.
options: { ok: true, value: '₦2500' } { ok: false, error: 'account-not-found' }
{ ok: true, value: '₦2500' } { ok: false, error: '₦NaN' }
{ ok: true, value: 2500 } { ok: false, error: 'account-not-found' }
₦2500 account-not-found

questions.q: In a function returning Result<{ balance: number }, TransferError>, why may you write if (!from.ok) return from; when from is Result<Account, "account-frozen">?
questions.explain: After narrowing, from is { ok: false; error: "account-frozen" }. That object is a valid failed Result of any value type whose error union includes "account-frozen".
options: Because TypeScript ignores return types inside if blocks
Because a failed result has no value, and its error code is one of the TransferError codes, so it fits the wider type
Because Account and { balance: number } are the same
Because return converts the value automatically

questions.q: What does the parameter messages: Record<E, string> in toResponse<T, E extends string>(result, messages) enforce?
questions.explain: Record<E, string> is an object type with exactly one required property per member of E. Leaving one out is a compile error at the endpoint.
options: That messages are shorter than 100 characters
That there is a message for every error code in E, so a new code cannot reach clients without one
That E is string
Nothing; Record is only documentation

questions.q: Why do transaction-history APIs often use a cursor (nextCursor) instead of page numbers?
questions.explain: With offsets, a new item at the top pushes everything down one position. A cursor names a specific item, so the next page starts right after it regardless of inserts.
options: Cursors are shorter than numbers
New transactions arriving between requests shift numbered pages, so items get repeated or skipped; a cursor continues after the last item seen
Page numbers cannot be typed in TypeScript
Cursors make responses smaller

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first page holds T1 and T2, and its cursor is the last id, T2. The second page starts after T2, holds only T3, and there is nothing more, so its cursor is null.
options: 2 T2 [ 'T3' ] null
2 T3 [ 'T3' ] null

questions.q: What does mapPage<T, U>(page: Page<T>, fn: (item: T) => U): Page<U> protect against?
questions.explain: The helper changes only the items and keeps everything else, so every endpoint that reshapes a page keeps its cursor by construction.
options: Pages with too many items
Endpoints that transform items (for example to public summaries) and forget to copy the paging metadata such as nextCursor
Items of the wrong type being stored in the database
Slow map calls

questions.q: What makes ApiResponse<T, E> a good envelope for every endpoint?
questions.explain: One discriminated union shape means one client helper can unwrap every response, and the error codes per endpoint are known at compile time.
options: It lets each endpoint invent its own shape
A status discriminant with either typed data or an error whose code is a closed union, so clients handle every endpoint the same way
It avoids using HTTP status codes
It hides errors from the client

questions.q: Why does TtlCache<K, V extends {} | null> forbid undefined as a value type?
questions.explain: {} is every value except null and undefined; adding | null allows null back. The constraint turns an ambiguous API into a compile error.
options: Because Map cannot store undefined
Because get returns undefined for a miss, so a cached undefined would look like a miss and the loader would run every time
Because {} means "empty object"
Because undefined cannot be serialised

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call loads and caches until time 1000. At 500 the entry is still fresh. At 1500 it has expired, so the loader runs a second time.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Map compares object keys by identity: the second object literal is a different object, so the lookup misses. Composite cache keys are safer as strings.
options: undefined 1550
1550 undefined
undefined undefined

questions.q: Why does the cache take a now: () => number parameter defaulting to Date.now?
questions.explain: Injecting the clock makes time-based behaviour deterministic and fast to test, while production code simply uses the default.
options: Because Date.now is not available in Node.js
So tests can move time forward with a fake clock, instead of waiting for entries to expire
So the cache can store dates
Because generic classes cannot call global functions

questions.q: In emit<K extends keyof Events>(name: K, payload: Events[K]), what does Events[K] give?
questions.explain: K is inferred from the name you pass, and indexing the event map with it picks that event's payload type. Wrong names and wrong payloads both become compile errors.
options: The name of the event
The payload type for exactly the event named by K
A union of all payload types
The listener function type

questions.q: Why does TransferService take a Repository<Account> rather than a MemoryRepository<Account>?
questions.explain: Depending on the interface keeps the service independent of storage. Anything that implements Repository<Account> fits.
options: Because classes cannot be constructor parameters
So a database-backed repository or a test fake can be passed without changing the service
Because interfaces are faster than classes
Because MemoryRepository cannot be generic

questions.q: A type-test file contains // @ts-expect-error above accounts.findBy("frozen", "yes"). What happens if someone loosens findBy so the line compiles?
questions.explain: @ts-expect-error requires an error on the next line. When the error disappears, the directive itself becomes an error, which is exactly how type-level tests catch APIs that stopped refusing bad calls.
options: Nothing; the comment is ignored
tsc reports an unused @ts-expect-error directive, so the type test fails
The line is deleted from the output
The program throws at runtime

questions.q: Why should a generic repository's runtime tests use at least two different entity types, such as one with string ids and one with number ids?
questions.explain: Generic code runs the same JavaScript for every type, but the values differ. Map.get("101") misses a number key 101, and only a test with numeric ids shows it.
options: Because Vitest requires two types per test
Because a bug may appear only for one kind of type argument, for example a lookup that turns ids into strings
Because TypeScript erases generics only for the first type
It is not useful; one type proves the code works for all

questions.q: Replace the return-only generic with a keyof design: getSetting<K extends keyof Settings>(key: K): Settings[K], with no assertion.
questions.explain: The key now decides the type: Settings[K] is number for the limit and "NGN" | "USD" for the currency. Typing store as Settings makes the lookup checked, so no as is needed.

questions.q: Write unwrapOr<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>, fallback: NoInfer<T>): T and use it to show a balance, or 0 when the lookup failed.
questions.explain: NoInfer makes the result decide T, so a fallback of the wrong type (say "none") is a compile error instead of widening T to number | string.

questions.q: Write andThen: if the result succeeded, call fn with its value and return what fn returns; otherwise return the failure unchanged. Then chain the two checks.
questions.explain: The failure branch returns result as it is: a failed result has no value, so it fits Result<U, E | F>. The error type of the chain is the union of both steps' codes.

questions.q: Write mapPage<T, U> that transforms the items and keeps nextCursor. Use it to turn accounts into public summaries { id, owner }.
questions.explain: Spreading the page keeps every metadata field, and only items is replaced. U is inferred from the callback's return value, so the result is a Page<{ id: string; owner: string }> with the balance removed.

questions.q: Write toResponse: a success becomes { status: "success", data }, a failure becomes { status: "error", error: { code, message } } with the message from the messages record.
questions.explain: After result.ok is checked, result.error has type E, so messages[result.error] is a string without any assertion: Record<E, string> has a key for every code.

questions.q: Add once to the emitter: it subscribes a listener that removes itself before running, so it only ever sees the first event.
questions.explain: The wrapper calls the unsubscribe function returned by on before running your listener. Because emit iterates over a copy, removing a listener mid-loop is safe.

questions.q: Write all<T, E>(results): return { ok: true, value: [...] } with every value when all succeeded, otherwise the first failure unchanged.
questions.explain: Stop at the first failure and return it as it is; a failed result has no value, so it fits Result<T[], E>. Only when every result succeeded is the array of values returned.
questions.expected:
{ ok: true, value: [ 5000, 1200 ] }
{ ok: false, error: 'invalid-amount' }
